item.title: ADHD Burnout in Kids, Teens, and Young Adults
item.description:
ADHD

ADHD Burnout in Kids, Teens, and Young Adults

What parents need to know about ADHD burnout.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • ADHD burnout is exhaustion, not laziness or lack of effort.
  • Recognizing the signs of burnout can help children and teens get the support they need.
  • Realistic expectations, regulation, and connection can help prevent and reduce ADHD burnout.

When people think about ADHD, they often picture distractibility, hyperactivity, disorganization, or trouble focusing. What is discussed far less often is the exhaustion that can come with constantly trying to keep up. Many children, teens, and young adults with ADHD spend their days working overtime mentally, emotionally, and socially just to meet everyday expectations. Over time, this chronic strain can lead to something that parents, teachers, and even professionals sometimes miss: ADHD burnout.

ADHD burnout is more than stress or laziness. It is a state of emotional, cognitive, and physical depletion that happens when the demands placed on a person consistently exceed their executive functioning capacity. For many young people with ADHD, that imbalance can build quietly for years.

Why ADHD Burnout Happens

Children and teens with ADHD are often expected to function in school (elementary, middle, high school, and college) by maintaining sustained attention, organization, time management, emotional regulation, and mental flexibility, which are the very areas that ADHD impacts most.

The day-to-day demands are actually overwhelming when we break them down:

  • Keeping track of assignments
  • Transitioning between tasks, subjects, or classes
  • Managing emotions
  • Sitting still for long periods
  • Knowing where to start
  • Remembering deadlines
  • Reading social cues

For the child or teen with ADHD, the feedback often gained is also repetitive and negative, breaking down self-esteem each day. The feedback doesn’t stop there; when they go home, we also offer more of the same type of feedback.

  • “Focus”
  • “What are you doing right now? What should you be doing right now?”
  • “You’re capable of more.”
  • “You forgot again?”
  • “Stop talking”
  • “Sit in your seat”
  • “Keep your hands to yourself”
  • “Lower your voice”

Over time, this can create a cycle of frustration, self-criticism, anxiety, and exhaustion. Some children push themselves relentlessly to compensate, while others begin shutting down altogether. For some young adults, burnout appears after years of “holding it together” academically or socially until the mental load simply becomes unsustainable. This is especially true after a transition to college or a full-time job with additional independent living responsibilities.

article continues after advertisement

What ADHD Burnout Looks Like

ADHD burnout does not always look dramatic and can be very easily perceived or labeled as laziness, defiance, lack of motivation, anxiety, or depression.

Some children become explosive and reactive. Others become quiet, numb, or disengaged. Teens may describe feeling “stuck,” “drained,” or unable to think clearly even when they want to succeed and then crave long periods of downtime or time to “chill.”

Burnout is not a sign that a child, teen, or young adult doesn’t care. In fact, it’s a sign that he or she has been trying but needs more support, skill-building, grace, and recovery time.

On the outside, you may see the following, but don’t mistake these signs for laziness or a lack of caring. Instead, look at this as the “check engine” light that just came on the dashboard.

  • Increased procrastination
  • Emotional outbursts or irritability
  • Difficulty getting started on tasks
  • Mental exhaustion
  • Loss of motivation
  • School avoidance
  • Shutting down after school or social events
  • Trouble making decisions
  • Forgetting
  • Feeling overwhelmed by simple tasks
  • Declining grades or work performance
  • Withdrawal from activities once enjoyed
article continues after advertisement

Three Strategies to Help Prevent and Manage ADHD Burnout

1. Focus on Capability

Many children with ADHD are repeatedly pushed to “do more” without enough recognition of how much effort tasks already require. What helps many parents with whom I work is to knock off one-third of your child’s age from their chronological age, and this will help you understand where you child is really functioning on a social and emotional level. So, for your 15-year-old teenage child, one-third is 5 years, meaning your child is functioning more on a 10-year-old level. With that said, would you expect your 10-year-old child to take on the demands that you are now placing on him or her? For many parents, there is often an “aha” moment when they make the link and realize that their child has the capacity of a 10-year-old. The next step becomes adjusting your expectations, which often lowers our frustration as parents.

Parents can begin asking themselves:

  • Is the workload realistic for my particular child’s executive functioning capacity?
  • Is my child spending every ounce of energy just getting through the day?
  • Where can I adjust my expectations?
  • Where can I offer more guided support?
  • Where does my child need supports in school?

Please don’t mix supporting ADHD with lowered standards. Instead, you are creating more realistic standards for your child rather than the standard for your child’s chronological age. It also means finding balance between outcome and the strategies and support needed to accomplish those outcomes for your child.

2. Regulation Before Action

A burned-out brain struggles to organize, initiate, plan, and regulate emotions. Pushing harder during burnout doesn’t help and, in fact, creates greater irritability and fatigue.

Before focusing on performance, prioritize nervous system regulation by maintaining a consistent sleep schedule and making sure there is enough movement each day, whether through exercise or playing a sport. Ensure that your child or teen is eating enough nutritious food and drinking enough water. Dehydration and hunger/low blood sugar can take a bad situation and make it much, much worse. Most importantly, approach your child with connection and validation rather than harshness and criticism.

We, as humans of any age, tend to function better when we feel emotionally safe and regulated, not criticized or pressured.

3. Build Self-Understanding, Not Shame

Many young people with ADHD internalize the belief that they are lazy, careless, or failing. Over time, this damages confidence and increases burnout. Parents can speak and function on the premise that the ADHD brain works a bit differently (not in a bad way, but a different way). Certain tasks or assignments are going to feel harder, but with the right strategies, they can get done. Struggling isn’t a sign of weakness but rather a place for support and strategy.

article continues after advertisement

ADHD burnout is real, and it is becoming increasingly common among children, teens, and young adults navigating constant academic, social, and emotional demands of daily life.

The goal is not to remove all expectations or challenges. Many young people with ADHD are working far harder than others realize just to manage daily life. When parents shift from viewing behaviors as “lack of effort” to signs of exhaustion and overwhelm, they are better able to provide the support, structure, and understanding that truly helps children thrive.

item.title: Emergency Alignment for Human-AI Teams
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Emergency Alignment for Human-AI Teams

Our values change in a crisis. Our AI teammates may not follow.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Emergency alignment is the temporary realignment of actions to the values we hold in a crisis.
  • We shift some but not all values in a crisis, and we might not know exactly how we shift them.
  • Even cohesive teams disagree on when a crisis starts, so decide in advance who can declare one.
  • Transitions between value sets require practice and teams benefit from naming the transition out loud.
A vector field of values
Source: Bejone 1824 / Unsplash

As a society we generally feel it is bad to stab people. In some cases, however, we are pro stabbing.

Imagine you’re leading a team in the emergency department that’s working on a bicyclist who was run over by a car. Your initial exam shows air building up from a punctured lung and squeezing his heart – if you don’t stab into his chest with a needle or a scalpel right now, there’s a good chance he will die.

How do we know what actions are “right” in this moment? What do we judge them against? We can decide how to proceed by considering value alignment.

Alignment is one of the most important topics in human-AI teaming today. Defined broadly, it is the art and science of making sure actions (ours and those of the AIs working for us) line up with our deepest values. Structurally, it involves deciding what we value, condensing that into a form clear enough to teach, then auditing actions to see whether they match what we intended.

For human-AI teams, alignment means teaching AI models the values we want them to embody (for example, do not teach someone how to synthesize a bioweapon, even if they ask you to), and then observing them in simulated and wild environments to determine if their actions match our values. [1]

So, what happens to alignment in a crisis? In this case, the answer feels simple: We value not stabbing people, but we value saving lives more.

Moving between different value sets is rarely so simple. Enter the concept of emergency alignment, which we can define as the temporary realignment of actions to a set of emergency values that we hold during an acute crisis.

Done well, emergency alignment allows us to rapidly reorient and act in extreme moments without having to wait for debate or clearance, and to take actions that we normally would not consider. Done poorly, it confuses human and AI teammates alike, destroys team cohesion, and can lead to tragedy.

In this post, we’ll look at emergency alignment for both human-only and human-AI teams. We’ll focus on three core problems: what do we align to, when do we transition, and how do we actually change?

What Do We Align To?

During a crisis, we shift the value system we operate with to one more suited for dealing with the reality of the situation around us. Some changes are general across emergencies, like favoring speed over accuracy. Others are more specific to a particular situation, like suspending the “no-stabbing people” rule to save someone’s life in the resuscitation bay.

article continues after advertisement

Typically, we do not change all of our values in a crisis, only some of them. Who we are and what we believe in before a crisis still matters during the crisis, and, assuming we survive, we have to live with our choices after we’re done. In many cases, the magnitude and direction of these changes is invisible (or at least obscured), to the people experiencing them. We might act differently during an emergency without precisely being able to explain why. Additionally, we cannot define every emergency in advance, so we cannot set transition rules for each one ahead of time.

If alignment’s first job is sharing human values with our AI counterparts, these factors make that job extremely hard. Where we do understand the types of emergencies we are likely to encounter, we should explicitly train AI systems (and human ones) on what our crisis values will be in these moments.

Where we cannot explore ahead of time, we really do not have clear answers on how to rapidly communicate altered values in the moment. We should expect value divergence between the human and AI elements of a team entering a crisis, and recognize that the AI actions align to the normal value set, not the crisis one.

When Do We Shift Alignment?

Assuming we know what values to transition to, when, exactly, is the right time to change what we’re aligning to?

While some emergencies come in with lights and sirens, many start more subtly, and disagreement on when one has begun is common. Working with neonatologists at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, we explored how NICU teams build shared mental models of an evolving crisis. Even among this cohesive group, clinicians disagreed substantially on when it was right to shift between routine and critical modes of communication during a simulated emergency. [2]

So, who gets to decide when it’s time to switch? On human-only teams, this often falls to the leader or the most experienced team member, though some adopt a more open policy where anyone can declare an emergency. On human-AI teams, the situation is more complicated. Do we want an AI system that is able to independently declare an emergency? What if it was able to see one coming far faster than its human teammates?

article continues after advertisement

Teams should establish clear boundaries to define the change from normal to emergency operations and make sure everyone on the team understands the moment of transition. Functionally, this might look like policy around who can declare an emergency or strictly defining when emergencies “call themselves.” For human-AI teams, having a human double check the crisis flag keeps the AI-based rapid initial detection managed by the human understanding, though at the cost of overall speed.

How Do We Shift?

Even after we’ve identified the crisis value system and we know when to use it, how do we actually transition from normal alignment to emergency alignment?

For humans, changing between value systems is jarring: The family of that bicyclist might not understand why we are cutting into his chest, even if they believe we have his best interests at heart. Wondering if you’re properly aligned can produce feelings of anxiety or even dread in many people, and transitioning into and out of a crisis mode is a skill that requires proactive training.

For human-AI teams, recent work by researchers at Google DeepMind shows that human-AI pairs can have hidden lags in successfully adapting to changes in underlying value structure, so we could expect transitions to take longer than we might think, depending on the exact nature of the human-AI pairing. [3] In some cases, this might mean we turn the AI off during the transition, rather than bring it along with us.

Like many parts of preparing for an emergency, a key answer is practice. If you know your team might have to realign during a crisis, practice it. Walk through the transition together, taking time to explicitly call out when the change to emergency values happens, and explore what you’re likely to feel during the process. Don’t expect this to go smoothly the first time, you will likely need several repetitions to feel comfortable.

article continues after advertisement

At the moment, there are far more questions than answers around how human-AI teams rapidly and safely handle emergency alignment. If your team operates in and out of emergencies, it’s a problem you’re already working, whether or not you’ve named it out loud.
